title: mcp.task.v1: a Task of the Control MCP server, derived from a turn or from a run
description: How the Control MCP server answers for a Task. A Task is not stored anywhere of its own: it is DERIVED, at the moment it is asked for, from the daemon's records and its event log, so it survives a restart of the MCP server and of the daemon. This record is that derivation, and conformance/rules.py (task_of_run, task_of_turn) states it as code that the vectors in vectors/task.derivation check; the server maps the fields onto the wire names of the protocol version it speaks. A Task has one of two sources, named in 'source'. SOURCE turn, for a turn of a session: task_id is the turn_id; the status comes from the turn's state (queued or running -> 'working', or 'input_required' while an approval is pending for it; 'ended' -> 'completed', with the turn's outcome carried here so a caller can tell 'done' from 'waiting'; 'failed' -> 'failed'; 'interrupted' or 'stopped' -> 'cancelled'); the result is the turn's own result and the expiry the turn's own. It is never derived from the latest result of a run that several turns share. Cancelling a turn's Task is an interrupt of that turn, not a Stop: the Task is cancelled when the turn's outcome is interrupted, and the worker may live on. SOURCE run, for a run started with run.start and no session: such a run has no session and no turn record, so task_id is the run_id and the status comes from the run's view. Starting, running, a Stop pending and an unobservable unit -> 'working' ('input_required' while an approval is pending); a Stop that was asked and is not confirmed (the view says stop_pending, or carries a stop record, or both) sets cancel_requested and leaves the status as it was; 'stopped' -> 'cancelled', only once the Stop is confirmed; ended with a result -> 'completed' when the result carries no code and says ok, 'failed' with the result's code when it carries one, and result_ref is the run id (the whole result stays in run.status); a result that breaks the route contract's own rule (ok exactly when there is no code) is never 'completed': it is 'failed', with its code, or with the code result_invalid when it has none (result_invalid truthfully says the retained result cannot be projected; it must not invent an engine failure reason); ended with NO result kept -> 'failed', code result_unavailable; a start that never launched -> 'failed', code start_failed, with the code of the record's start_error as the detail when the record carries one and a null detail when it does not (the reason is not durable until the lane that owns Stop writes it; a Task never invents one); lost at a reboot -> 'failed', code lost_reboot. working for unknown means no terminal outcome is known, not observed progress. failed/lost_reboot reports loss of the run's continuity, not proof that an external effect failed or did not happen. A Task of a run has no turn outcome, and its expiry is null until a retention rule exists (PROVISIONAL; the MCP lane checks it against the Tasks conformance run). BOTH: created_at is the time of the event that establishes the creation of the run or the turn, and updated_at the time of its latest state.changed; they are times the core logged, and each is null when the log holds no such event. Task/transcript origin comes from retained creation metadata or the actual creation event. A retained tail or replay.gap is not a creation time; if the true origin is unavailable, Task created_at is null. Task created_at comes from retained creation metadata or an event that establishes creation of that entity. Position 1 and absence of an earlier replay.gap are retention checks, not proof of creation. In particular, state.changed with reason snapshot describes an entity that already existed when logging began and is not its creation event; reconcile likewise does not establish creation. If no retained fact establishes the origin, created_at is null. updated_at may still use a later retained state change. The rule (conformance/rules.py, _log_times) takes the log as it is retained. The event that establishes creation is the entity's first state.changed in the log when its reason is commit, and only where the log is whole up to it: it begins at position 1, no position before the event is missing, and no replay.gap stands before it. An event of another type that names the run or the turn establishes nothing. No record of this version carries creation metadata in the timestamp form, so the log is the only source today: a run that already existed when logging began (its log begins with a snapshot) has a null created_at. An approval is never answered through a Task: 'input_required' tells the client that a person must answer on a surface that draws approvals.

task_id.description: The turn_id for source 'turn', the run_id for source 'run'.

source.description: What the Task is derived from.

run_id.description: The run. For source 'turn' it is the turn's run, null while the turn is not bound to one.

outcome.description: The turn's outcome once it has ended; null before that, and always null for a Task of a run.

cancel_requested.description: True while a Stop has been asked and is not confirmed.

status_message.description: A sentence for a person, written by the server. The derivation does not decide it.

created_at.description: The time of the event that establishes the creation of this run or turn (its first state.changed, seen as it was made), as the core logged it; null when nothing retained establishes it.

updated_at.description: The time of the latest state.changed in the log for this run or turn; null when the log holds none.

expires_at.description: The turn's expires_at: when its result can no longer be read. null means for as long as the record is kept, and it is always null for a Task of a run.

poll_interval_ms.description: How long a client should wait before asking again; null when the daemon gives no advice. The derivation does not decide it.

result.description: For source 'turn', the turn's result as the session record keeps it. For source 'run', the code and detail of the run's result with the run id as result_ref, or the typed failure when there is no result to read.

A Task's result. code is null when the work succeeded and a typed code when it did not. detail says more and may carry engine text, which is untrusted; it is null where nothing more is known (a start that never launched and left no recorded reason, a result that was not kept). result_ref names where the full result can be read, or is null when there is none.
